article.overview: A biological sample preservation system is a storage facility that keeps biological material, such as cells, tissues or reproductive material, at very low temperatures for long periods so that it remains viable. The best-documented lunar concept for this payload class is a 2024 proposal for a passive lunar biorepository. Its authors propose a vault on the Moon that would hold live, cryopreserved samples at or below -196 °C, using the cold lunar environment rather than powered refrigeration [1]. No such vault has been flown, and the proposal has no dated mission [1][2]. Cold-stowage freezers already operate on the International Space Station (ISS). The Minus Eighty Laboratory Freezer for ISS (MELFI) is the most relevant operating example, and it is described in the physical specifications section [3][4].
article.description: Biological preservation at low temperature is called cryopreservation. Cooling living material to very low temperatures slows or effectively stops its metabolism, which allows it to be stored for long periods. The 2024 lunar biorepository proposal states that long-term storage of living cells from animal species requires temperatures at -196 °C or below [1]. The proposal focuses first on animal skin samples, cultured as fibroblast cells. The authors describe an exemplar system based on cryopreserved pelvic fins from the Starry Goby (Asterropteryx semipunctata) [1]. In the paper's figure, the fins are placed dry in a cryovial with a sterile damp sponge [1]. The paper does not specify a capsule design and says the radiation-reducing packaging has not yet been identified [1]. Because no lunar system exists, the physical description relies on the proposal text and on documented ISS hardware. It does not describe a flight design.
article.scientific_purpose_and_applications: The stated purpose of the lunar biorepository is to protect Earth's biodiversity by storing prioritised taxa as live cryopreserved samples [1][2]. The Smithsonian-led proposal names candidate groups including pollinators, primary producers, threatened and endangered animals, and wild relatives of domesticated organisms, with an initial focus on species most affected by climate change in the next 50 years [2]. The paper also names possible future additions such as invertebrate larvae, gametes (oocytes and sperm) and plants [1]. The proposal links the work to space exploration. It suggests that cells held at -196 °C may have little metabolism and so may escape much of the effect of lunar gravity, but the authors present this as reasoning rather than tested data [1]. Applications of stored samples include future research on cell survival in space conditions and recovery of genetic material if species are lost on Earth [1][2]. These applications are stated goals in the proposal, not demonstrated results.
article.operating_principle: The proposed lunar system is passive. The paper describes a design that does not depend on generating power to maintain ultralow temperature, and contrasts it with a proposed lunar ark that would depend on solar energy for power and to keep it cold [1]. The cold source is the lunar environment itself. The paper refers to permanently shadowed regions and seasonal conditions at or below -196 °C near the lunar poles as cold sources [1][2]. This article does not recommend any lunar site. Radiation is the second key constraint. The paper says that once samples are surrounded by about 1 metre of regolith, much of the cosmic and solar radiation is mitigated [1]. It lists other possible barriers, including water, lead, cement and regolith [1]. During cryopreservation, the authors propose antioxidant cocktails combined with protease inhibitors to protect the cells chemically [1]. The operating principle of the MELFI freezer on ISS is different. It is an active, powered freezer. NASA's technical record describes an internal nitrogen gas cycle [4]. A secondary summary describes a reverse Brayton cycle using nitrogen as the working fluid [6]. The primary sources reviewed do not confirm the exact cycle type.
article.scientific_importance: The scientific importance of a biological sample preservation system lies in keeping biological material in a stable, viable state so it can be studied later. For a lunar system, the proposal's central argument is that the Moon's cold, dry and radiation-exposed environment could provide long-term storage without continuous refrigeration power, provided shielding and packaging are adequate [1]. The paper frames the program as a decades-long effort [1]. The paper reports no new experimental data. It states that 'No new data were generated or analysed' [1]. Microgravity testing reported in the paper was performed on cryopreserved cardiac cells for only months on Earth, and the authors state that long-term effects are not known [1].

physical_specifications.note: There is no universal specification for a biological sample preservation system. Storage temperature, capacity, mass and power depend on whether a system is an active ISS freezer or a passive lunar vault. The two examples are not directly comparable. The MELFI is a powered ISS freezer. The lunar concept is a passive vault with no published hardware design.

examples.name: Minus Eighty Laboratory Freezer for ISS (MELFI)
examples.total_capacity_reported: 300, unit not stated on the JAXA page [3]; reported as 300 litres with four 75-litre dewars by a secondary Wikipedia article [6], not confirmed by a primary source reviewed.
examples.mass_reported_secondary: 730 kg reported by a secondary Wikipedia article [6]; unverified in primary sources reviewed.
examples.cooling_method: Internal nitrogen gas cycle as stated by NASA [4]. A reverse Brayton cycle with nitrogen working fluid is reported by a secondary source only [6].
examples.flight_history: First unit (MELFI-1) launched in 2006; the other two units launched in 2008 and 2009 according to NASA's technical record [4]. A secondary Wikipedia article gives the final unit as flown on STS-131 in 2010 [6]. The sources disagree on the later launch date; the NASA record is used here.

examples.name: Proposed passive lunar biorepository
examples.type: Proposed concept (no hardware built, flown or tested in lunar conditions)
examples.cold_source: Lunar environment, with permanently shadowed regions and seasonal cold conditions cited [1][2].
examples.shielding: About 1 metre of regolith is the only specific thickness given in the primary paper [1]. The Smithsonian page describes samples placed 'a few meters belowground' [2]. The two statements disagree and neither is a design parameter.
examples.cryocooler: No cryocooler is named in the primary paper [1]. Secondary coverage mentions a Stirling cryocooler, which the primary text does not support.
examples.capsule_design: Not specified. The radiation-reducing packaging has not yet been identified [1].

physical_specifications.dimensions_and_proportions: No published dimensions exist for a lunar biological sample preservation system. The MELFI external dimensions were not stated in the primary sources reviewed. A lunar vault's size would depend on its sample capacity, radiation shielding thickness, insulation and burial or cover arrangement. None of these is specified in the proposal [1][2].
physical_specifications.mass_and_weight: No published mass exists for the proposed lunar vault. Secondary Wikipedia coverage reports 730 kg for the MELFI [6], but this figure is unverified in primary sources reviewed. Mass would drive launch, landing and deployment requirements, and none has been defined for the lunar concept [1].
physical_specifications.power_requirements: The MELFI is powered. Primary power figures were not stated in the sources reviewed [3][4]. The proposed lunar vault is designed to be passive and to need no power to maintain ultralow temperature [1]. Power needs for monitoring or any heater or data system are not specified.

article.environmental_and_operational_requiremen: The proposed system must hold samples at or below -196 °C without active power, so it depends on the cold environment and on insulation and packaging [1]. It must also withstand radiation, and the paper cites regolith cover as one of the main protections [1]. During transit, samples face temperature changes and radiation. If samples were returned to Earth, the paper estimates about three days of solar and cosmic radiation exposure each way, and delays could mean several months of exposure [1]. The paper proposes testing packaging and radiation sensitivity on Earth before any space testing [1].
article.limitations: No lunar system has flown, and no lunar test is described in the sources reviewed [1][2]. The proposal is a forum piece that reports no new experimental data [1]. The capsule design, radiation-reducing packaging and any cryocooler are not specified [1]. Long-term viability of cryopreserved cells after spaceflight and lunar exposure is unknown [1]. The ISS testing step is conditional ('if possible') [1]. The 2024 Smithsonian webpage and the paper disagree on burial depth [1][2].

transportation_and_deployment.overview: A lunar biorepository would be a surface storage payload. It would need Earth integration, launch, lunar transfer, landing, deployment and then long-term storage. The sources reviewed do not describe a lander interface, deployment method, power or data interface, or mass budget for such a system [1][2].
transportation_process: Package cryopreserved samples in radiation-reducing packaging. The packaging is not yet identified [1].
Test packaging and radiation sensitivity in Earth-based laboratories [1].
Conditionally, test packaging on the ISS before lunar storage [1].
Launch the payload and transfer it towards the Moon. No vehicle or lander is specified [1].
Land the payload on the lunar surface. No lander interface is verified [1].
Place the vault under regolith cover. The proposal describes the shielding effect of about 1 metre of regolith, but not the emplacement method [1].
transportation_and_deployment.deployment_methods: The sources reviewed do not describe a deployment method for the lunar vault. Burial under regolith is the main protection proposed, but how the vault would be emplaced or covered is not described [1].
transportation_and_deployment.historical_examples: No lunar biological sample preservation system has been deployed. The MELFI is an ISS example of cold-stowage hardware that has been operated in space [3][4].
transportation_and_deployment.compatibility_assessment: No lander, spacecraft or rover compatibility has been verified for a lunar biological sample preservation system, and none is assumed here. The return chain would need radiation-protected packaging, since the paper estimates about three days of radiation each way for returned samples, with longer exposure if delayed [1].

article.historical_significance: The MELFI freezer has operated as ISS cold-stowage equipment since 2006 and provides a documented example of spaceflight preservation hardware [3][4]. The 2024 lunar biorepository proposal is historically significant as a published proposal for a passive, off-Earth biological repository [1][2]. It has not yet produced an operating system.
article.limitations_and_uncertainties: The lunar concept has no published mass, dimensions, power, capsule design or lifetime [1][2]. The paper gives no dated mission, launch date or ISS schedule for the proposed tests [1]. The Smithsonian page and the paper disagree on burial depth ('a few meters' versus about 1 metre of regolith) [1][2]. A cryocooler and a 1–2 year timeline appear in secondary news coverage, but the primary paper does not support them [1]. The MELFI mass (730 kg), total capacity in litres and the final-unit launch date come from a secondary source and are unverified in primary documents [3][4][6]. The primary MELFI dimensions, mass and power were not available in the sources reviewed. The NASA image asset URL was taken from the source page's download link and was not separately fetched.

image_handling.url_policy: All image_url and source_page_url values in this file have query strings and fragments removed. Section-level image objects are repeated intentionally so each article section can render its own images without resolving IDs against the master gallery.

data_quality_notes: Only one verified source-page image was found. Overview, transportation and lunar-example sections have no images.
The NASA image asset URL was taken from the source page's Download link and was not separately fetched. direct_image_assets_verified_from_official_pages is therefore false.

Burial depth conflicts between the primary paper (about 1 m of regolith, reference 1) and the Smithsonian page ('a few meters belowground', reference 2). Both are reported; neither is a design parameter.
A Stirling cryocooler and a 1–2 year timeline appear in secondary news coverage only. They are excluded because the primary paper names no cryocooler and describes a decades-long program.

MELFI mass (730 kg), total capacity in litres (300 L, with 75 L dewars) and the final-unit launch year (2010) come from the secondary Wikipedia article. The NASA record gives the other units as launched in 2008 and 2009, so the sources disagree on the final unit.
MELFI primary dimensions, mass and power were not available in the sources reviewed. The ESA factsheet was not reachable by search.

Primary paper states 'In 4.5% of the Moon's southern pole, seasonal temperature variation is stable year-round at or below -196 C' as quoted from the fetched text. This was not cross-checked against the PDF and is not used as a specification.
